extracted.intended_audience: general readers, writers, and students interested in rhetoric and stylistic devices
extracted.subtask_description: A reference listing rhetorical figures (each treated as an 'element of eloquence') with short definitions and examples, intended to help readers identify and use these devices to craft memorable English phrases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alliteration
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeating the sound of the first consonant in a series of words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: 'Whereat, with blade, with bloody blameful blade, He bravely broached his boiling bloody breast;' (Shakespeare). Used for sonic emphasis; deliberate overuse noted as a stylistic choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polyptoton
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of one word as different parts of speech or in different grammatical forms; applies where words derived from the same root are used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Related to antanaclasis when the same word is repeated in a different sense. Example (Shakespeare): repetition of root-derived forms. Page notes overlap with antanaclasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antithesis
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of opposites for contrasting effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'It was the best of times, it was the worst of times.' (Dickens). Used to sharpen contrast and highlight difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merism
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference to one thing by an enumeration of its parts, or by a list of synonyms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forsyth focuses on the first definition (enumeration of parts). Example: 'Cannon to right of them, Cannon to left of them, Cannon in front of them' (Tennyson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Blazon
rubrics_metrics.description: The tradition in poetry of praising a woman by using metaphors to describe distinct parts of her body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Called 'extended merism, the dismemberment of the loved one.' Example: lines from Thomas Watson's Hekatompathia. A genre-specific poetic device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synaesthesia
rubrics_metrics.description: Where one sense is described in terms of another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Eduard Hanslick's criticism of Tchaikovsky's Violin Concerto as 'music that stinks to the ear.' Used to create striking sensory cross-mapping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aposiopesis
rubrics_metrics.description: When a sentence is deliberately left unfinished, with the ending to be supplied by the audience's imagination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creates impression of unwillingness or inability to continue. Example (King Lear): 'I will have such revenges on you both, that the world shall ...' (Shakespeare).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperbaton
rubrics_metrics.description: Changing the logical order of words in a sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Stone walls do not a prison make' (Lovelace) versus the natural 'Stone walls do not make a prison'; can create emphasis or a poetic effect (Forsyth notes the example is 'factually incorrect').

rubrics_metrics.name: Anadiplosis
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition of the last word of a preceding clause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (Bible/Romans): 'tribulation worketh patience, and patience, experience, and experience, hope...' Builds chain-like linkage between clauses for emphasis or progression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodic Sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: A sentence that is not complete grammatically before the final clause or phrase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Rudyard Kipling's poem If—. Used to withhold the main clause for suspense or rhetorical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotaxis and Parataxis
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrast between hypotaxis (complex style using many subordinate clauses) and parataxis (style of short, simple sentences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forsyth contrasts the two styles as alternatives in sentence construction; choice affects rhythm, complexity, and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diacope
rubrics_metrics.description: The close repetition of a word or phrase, separated by a word or words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forsyth cites 'Bond, James Bond' as memorable because of diacope — repetition separated by intervening material. Emphasizes how phrasing creates memorability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical Questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions used without the expectation of an answer, or to achieve various rhetorical purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forsyth divides them into types: (1) asked with no answer expected (e.g., 'Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?'), (2) questions with purpose but no real answer ('What's the point?'), (3) questions asked to audiences expecting a particular response (political rally examples), (4) questions immediately answered by the questioner ('You ask, what is our aim? ... Victory!'), and (5) questions where both parties know the answer (e.g., policeman to motorist). Notes exceptions (Monty Python example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hendiadys
rubrics_metrics.description: For emphasis an adjective-noun form is replaced by a noun-and-noun form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: instead of 'I'm going to the noisy city' say 'I'm going to the noise and the city.' Used to alter emphasis or rhythm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistrophe
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition of a word or words at the end of successive phrases, clauses or sentences for emphasis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (Steinbeck): Repeating 'I'll be there' at clause ends. Counterpart to anaphora; useful to create a refrain-like emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tricolon
rubrics_metrics.description: A sentence composed of three equal parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: France's motto 'Liberté, égalité, fraternité.' Often used for rhythm, balance, and persuasive effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epizeuxis
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition of a word or phrase for emphasis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (Fight Club): repeating 'you do not talk about Fight Club.' Immediate repetition to intensify emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syllepsis
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a word, used with two other parts of a sentence, must be understood differently in relation to each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Related to zeugma; uses a single word in two different senses to produce wit or concision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isocolon
rubrics_metrics.description: A sentence is composed of two (or more) parts equivalent in structure, length and rhythm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some sources suggest at least two equivalent parts. Produces parallel rhythm and balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enallage
rubrics_metrics.description: A deliberate grammatical mistake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Mistah Kurtz—he dead' (Conrad). Used for stylistic voice, dialect, or emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Versification
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion of the effect of different verse forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forsyth discusses how different verse structures shape effect and meaning; includes consideration of meter and stanza form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zeugma
rubrics_metrics.description: A series of clauses using the same verb (or a single verb applied to multiple objects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Related to syllepsis; can be used to create economy, surprise, or comic effect by applying one word to multiple senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paradox
rubrics_metrics.description: A logically false or impossible statement, used for emphasis or contrast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to highlight complexity or to force readers to reconsider assumptions; often striking when seemingly impossible statements carry truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chiasmus
rubrics_metrics.description: The symmetrical repetition of structure or wording.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Let us never negotiate out of fear, but let us never fear to negotiate.' (JFK). Balances ideas by reversing structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assonance
rubrics_metrics.description: The repetition of a vowel sound.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A sonic device used to create internal rhyme, mood, or musicality.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Fourteenth Rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing an unnecessarily specific number for something for emphasis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to create a sense of specificity or comic precision by giving an overly specific numeric detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catachresis
rubrics_metrics.description: The grammatically incorrect use of words for creative expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Hamlet saying 'I will speak daggers'—one cannot literally 'speak a dagger'. Used for striking, non-literal phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Litotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasizing a point by denying the opposite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understatement via negation (e.g., 'not bad' to mean 'good'); produces irony or restrained emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metonymy and Synecdoche
rubrics_metrics.description: Using something connected to the thing described, or a part of it, in place of the thing itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metonymy uses an associated term (e.g., 'the crown' for the monarchy); synecdoche uses a part for the whole or vice versa. Common figurative devices for economy and vividness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transferred Epithets
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying an adjective to the wrong noun, for effect (hypallage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: attributing a human quality to an inanimate object by transferring the epithet; creates freshness or surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleonasm
rubrics_metrics.description: Using superfluous or unnecessary words for emphasis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate redundancy used to intensify or clarify (e.g., 'I saw it with my own eyes').

rubrics_metrics.name: Epanalepsis
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition of a word or phrase at the beginning and end of a sentence or clause to emphasize circularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creates a framing or cyclical effect by bookending a sentence with the same word or phrase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personification
rubrics_metrics.description: Ascribing human actions or qualities to a non-human thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common in poetry and prose to make abstract or inanimate subjects relatable or vivid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperbole
rubrics_metrics.description: Exaggeration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used for strong emphasis or comic/poetic effect; ranges from plausible exaggeration to the extreme (see adynaton).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adynaton
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyperbole so extreme that it is completely impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A form of hyperbole taken to an impossible extreme to produce humor or emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prolepsis
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a pronoun at the start of a sentence, which reverses the normal order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Noted as a rhetorical reversal of expected word order; (page references prolepsis (rhetoric)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Congeries
rubrics_metrics.description: A bewildering list of adjectives or nouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A piling-up device that overwhelms or intensifies by accumulation of items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scesis Onomaton
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentences without a main verb.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A verbless or nominal sentence style used for emphasis, staccato rhythm, or rhetorical force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anaphora
rubrics_metrics.description: Starting each sentence with the same words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repetition at the beginning of successive clauses or sentences; creates rhythm, emphasis, and cohesion.
